subtopic: Preparing for a science or robotics competition
subtype: Approach: reading the rules and working backward from the deadline [Thinking]
passage: The rulebook had eleven pages, and we read every one out loud before touching a screwdriver. I'm Baljeet, and this is the part Sumit keeps asking about, so here it is. The event is on the 14th of March. We took a calendar and counted backwards: the last week stays empty, the week before is for rehearsal, two weeks for testing, three for building, two for design. We wrote each milestone on a chart on the lab wall, with a date. When the design ran a few days over, we didn't panic, because we knew exactly what to trim, and the empty final week was still there, untouched. Nobody pulled an all-nighter. The rules told us what mattered, and the dates told us when.

qa.q: How many pages did the rulebook have?
qa.a: The rulebook had eleven pages.

qa.q: What was Baljeet feeling when the design ran a few days over, and what kept things steady?
qa.a: Baljeet felt calm rather than panicked, because the team knew what to trim and the empty final week was still there.

qa.q: What could the team do if testing shows a big fault?
qa.a: They could trim a feature or use the free final week, since the schedule was built with room to spare.

qa.q: How might a teammate whose part runs slow feel under this plan?
qa.a: That teammate may feel less pressured, since the dates are shared and the plan has slack.

grounding: A team reads the rules and dates, then counts backward from the event to set milestones for design, build, testing and rehearsal, leaving the final week free.

subtopic: Preparing for a science or robotics competition
subtype: Approach: brainstorming many ideas then selecting one [Thinking]
passage: The lab was noisy with the carpentry class next door, and the team had exactly forty minutes before the bell. Ojas slapped down a pile of sticky notes. “Twenty designs, no judging, go.” Eshaan wrote a six-legged walker, Ojas drew a robot with a fan, someone sketched a wheeled arm that grabbed cans. By 4:15 twenty notes covered the whiteboard. Then Ojas drew three columns: cost, time, skills we have. Everyone stuck dots. The six-legged walker got lots of dots for excitement and none for time. The simple line-follower with three sensors angled to look ahead of the wheels won on all three. “Simple, but with a clever sensor layout,” Eshaan said. They stuck that note in the middle of the board just as the bell rang.

qa.q: How many designs did the team put on the whiteboard?
qa.a: Twenty notes covered the whiteboard.

qa.q: What was Eshaan feeling about the winning design?
qa.a: Eshaan was pleased and convinced, since Eshaan called it simple but with a clever sensor layout.

qa.q: What could the team do if the sensor arrangement fails?
qa.a: They could test other sensor angles or fall back to a plainer layout, keeping the simple base that scored well on cost, time and skill.

qa.q: How might the person who proposed the six-legged walker feel?
qa.a: That person may feel disappointed, but the dots gave the idea a fair hearing, so the loss is easier to accept. 🙂

grounding: Team members write twenty possible designs on sticky notes without judging, then vote on cost, time and skill and choose a simple line-follower with a clever sensor arrangement.

subtopic: Preparing for a science or robotics competition
subtype: Approach: building a minimum working prototype first [Action]
passage:
Naveen: chassis moves!! straight line works
Pema: does it turn?
Naveen: left is fine, right drifts 🙂
Pema: fix the right wheel first, no sensors yet
Naveen: agreed. if we bolt sensors on now we won't know if it's wiring or wheels
Pema: exactly. one thing at a time
Naveen: tightened the right wheel, it turns clean now
Pema: nice. now add ONE sensor and test
Naveen: done. it stops at the black line!
Pema: second one tomorrow
Naveen: so if it breaks we know it's the last thing we added
Pema: yep. and we always have a working robot to go back to 👍

qa.q: Which turn drifted on the chassis?
qa.a: Turning right drifted, while left was fine.

qa.q: Why does Naveen want to wait before adding sensors?
qa.a: Naveen worries the team would not know whether a fault is in the wiring or the wheels, and wants to trace problems easily.

qa.q: What could the team do if the second sensor breaks things?
qa.a: They could take the last sensor off and test again, since the base already worked.

qa.q: How might Pema see the step-by-step approach?
qa.a: Pema agrees and probably feels reassured, since every test builds on something already proven.

grounding: The team builds a basic chassis that moves and turns before adding sensors, so each new part is tested on something that already works.

subtopic: Preparing for a science or robotics competition
subtype: Approach: testing repeatedly and logging failures [Action]
passage: I'm Lalit. Hrithik and I ran our robot fifty times on the mock track and wrote every failure in a log: run number, what went wrong, our guess at why. Twenty-two of the fifty were the same thing, the left wheel wobbling loose. Eleven were sensor glare from the window. The rest looked random, and nobody wanted to chase the random ones. So we tightened the wheel, checked every screw before each run, and taped a card over the sensor as a shade. Then we ran fifty more. Forty-one finished. Looking back, the log changed how I felt about failing: from it keeps going wrong to here is the list, and we can fix number one first.

qa.q: How many of the fifty runs failed because of the loose left wheel?
qa.a: Twenty-two of the fifty were the wobbling left wheel.

qa.q: How did the log change what Lalit felt about the failures?
qa.a: Lalit went from feeling stuck to feeling hopeful, since a written list made the problems fixable one at a time.

qa.q: What else could the team try?
qa.a: They could test at different times of day or in another room to check the glare problem, and keep logging the results.

qa.q: How might Hrithik see the log?
qa.a: Hrithik may feel relieved to have evidence instead of arguments, since Hrithik helped run the tests and record them.

grounding: Students run the robot fifty times on a mock track, log each failure and cause, and fix the most frequent problem first, such as a loose wheel or sensor glare.

subtopic: Preparing for a science or robotics competition
passage:
Dear Rafiq Sir,
Here is our team update. We have split the work by strengths. Tarun does the wiring, because the soldering is always the neatest. Ishita writes the code. I am doing the documentation and will present to the judges, since I like explaining. But we don't work in separate boxes: every Friday we meet for twenty minutes, and each person explains their part in five minutes, and the rest ask questions. That way we can all describe the whole robot, even the parts we didn't build. Last Friday Ishita spotted a wiring idea from Tarun's explanation that saved a wire. Could you please look at our documentation draft on Monday?
Yours sincerely,
Neelam

qa.q: Who handles the code on the team?
qa.a: Ishita writes the code.

qa.q: How does Neelam seem to feel about the team's plan?
qa.a: Neelam seems confident and positive, since the plan uses everyone's strengths and still keeps shared understanding.

qa.q: What could the team do if one member is absent on the event day?
qa.a: The Friday explanations mean someone else already understands that part and could step in.

qa.q: How might Tarun feel about doing the wiring?
qa.a: Tarun is probably proud to be trusted with the work Tarun does best.

grounding: One student handles wiring, another coding, another documentation and presentation, and they swap ideas at weekly meetings.

subtopic: Preparing for a science or robotics competition
subtype: Approach: last-minute changes before the event [Pitfall]
passage:
“Jeevan, one more feature. Just a speed boost on the straights. Ten lines,” Parul said at ten p.m. in the lab.
“We haven't tested the current code on the real track since Tuesday.”
“It's tiny. The judges will be impressed.”
“It's the night before.”
“Fine, but let's push it.” Jeevan sighed and typed. They tested it twice on the desk, then packed up.
Next morning, first round. The robot shot forward, missed the first bend and rammed the wall. Parul stared. “The boost. It doesn't switch off at the corner.”
“I told—” Jeevan stopped. “No. It's our code. We can fix it for round two if we can.”
They had ninety seconds to reset. Nobody had saved the old version.

qa.q: Where did the robot go wrong in the first round?
qa.a: The robot missed the first bend and rammed the wall.

qa.q: What was Jeevan feeling when the robot failed?
qa.a: Jeevan was frustrated and about to say I told you, but held back and accepted the code was shared.

qa.q: What could the team do differently next time?
qa.a: They could freeze the code the night before, test every change on the real track and keep the old version saved.

qa.q: How might the judges see the first round?
qa.a: The judges see a robot that failed early, and may guess the team took a risk without testing.

grounding: The night before the event the team rewrites the control code to add a feature, never tests it fully and the robot misbehaves in the first round.

subtopic: Preparing for a science or robotics competition
subtype: Approach: one strong member doing everything [Pitfall]
passage: Coach's note, Harsha. Uday built the whole robot himself: wiring, code, chassis. The team watched. When teammates offered to help, he said it was quicker if he did it, and they let him. On competition day he was ill and stayed home. The other three stood at the table. They could not start the robot, and they could not answer the judges' questions about the sensors. We withdrew before the first run. I sat with the team afterwards and told them it was not about blame, and later I called Uday to say the same. Next entry, I have asked him to teach one part to each teammate before the event, and each of them to explain it back to the group.

qa.q: Who built the whole robot?
qa.a: Uday built the whole robot himself.

qa.q: How might Uday's teammates have felt standing at the table?
qa.a: They were probably helpless and embarrassed, since they could not start the robot or answer the judges' questions.

qa.q: What could the team do differently next time?
qa.a: They could share tasks and teach each teammate a part in advance, so anyone can run the robot and explain it.

qa.q: How might Uday feel when he hears what happened?
qa.a: Uday may feel guilty and disappointed that his illness left the team stuck, though Harsha tells him it is not about blame.

grounding: A gifted teen builds the whole project alone because it is quicker, and when he falls ill on the day, teammates cannot operate or explain it.

subtopic: Preparing for a science or robotics competition
subtype: Approach: contingency plan with spare parts [Thinking]
passage: So what's in our repair kit? Two spare batteries, a spare sensor, a roll of wire, a small screwdriver set, tape and a soldering pen. I'm Sabina, and our box has a list taped inside the lid. Seema is our repair person; her only job at the event is to fix things while the rest of us run the robot. In the second round a wire came loose and the robot froze on the line. Seema had it reconnected in four minutes with the tools from the box. Without the kit, that would have been the end of our day. Instead it was a small, annoying thing. The box weighs three kilos, and I would carry it for ten hours again.

qa.q: Who is the team's repair person?
qa.a: Seema is the team's repair person.

qa.q: How did the team feel about the loose wire?
qa.a: They were annoyed but calm, since it was a small annoying thing and not the end of the day.

qa.q: What else could the team pack in the kit?
qa.a: They could add a printed wiring diagram and spare screws, since the more they can fix quickly, the fewer surprises ruin a run.

qa.q: How might Seema see the repair role?
qa.a: Seema probably feels important and focused, since fixing things is her only job, though it may also bring some pressure.

grounding: The team packs spare batteries, sensors, wires and tools and assigns one member to repair, so a broken part is an inconvenience rather than the end of the run.

subtopic: Preparing for a science or robotics competition
subtype: Approach: reviewing the result and learning from the loss [Revision]
passage: The school van was leaving in twenty minutes, and the team was still in the empty competition hall, sitting on the floor with their fifth-place certificate between them. Mehak took out a notebook. “Two lists. What went well, what failed. Quick.” Aparna wrote: chassis strong, presentation clear, teamwork calm. Under failed: sensor calibration off in the second round, no time to retune, spare battery never tested. Mehak wrote at the bottom: next year, calibrate at the venue an hour early, and test every battery. Someone said, “Fifth means we're not last.” Mehak said, “Fifth means we know what to fix.” They tore the page out and put it inside the robot's box.

qa.q: Where did the team hold its meeting?
qa.a: The team sat on the floor of the empty competition hall.

qa.q: What was Mehak feeling about fifth place?
qa.a: Mehak felt motivated rather than defeated, treating the result as feedback.

qa.q: What could the team do to turn the list into progress?
qa.a: They could follow it next year: calibrate at the venue an hour early and test every battery, since a written plan is harder to forget.

qa.q: How might a teammate who said fifth means we're not last see the lists?
qa.a: That teammate may feel comforted at first, then see that the lists give real direction. 🙂

grounding: After finishing fifth, the team lists what went well and what failed, such as poor calibration, and writes changes for next year, treating the result as feedback.

subtopic: Preparing for a science or robotics competition
subtype: Approach: rehearsing the presentation to judges [Action]
passage:
Tuesday, 8 pm.
Practised our three-minute talk today in front of Thomas Sir and two parents. I talked too fast and used words like differential steering without explaining. Mrs Shah asked, “What does that mean?” and I froze. Thomas Sir said, “Good. That is exactly the question the judges will ask.” So I rewrote that part using a picture of a shopping trolley. Second time through, everyone nodded. We also listed likely questions: How much did it cost? (about 3,200 rupees) Is it safe near other people? (battery cut-off switch, no exposed wires). I wrote both answers on a card. Amma says her boy talks too fast when nervous, so I'm slowing down. Time: 2 min 50 sec.
— Zubin

qa.q: How long did the final version of the talk take?
qa.a: The time was 2 min 50 sec.

qa.q: What did Zubin feel when Mrs Shah asked what differential steering means?
qa.a: Zubin felt nervous and put on the spot, since he froze.

qa.q: What else could Zubin do before the judges?
qa.a: Zubin could practise with someone outside the team, since a new listener shows which parts are still unclear.

qa.q: How might Mrs Shah see the improved talk?
qa.a: Mrs Shah probably understands it much better, since she asked because the term was unclear and then saw everyone nod.

grounding: Students practise explaining their design in three minutes to a teacher and parents, refine unclear parts after questions and prepare answers about cost and safety.
